title: Mechanism details, the Slingerland make, and the stolen trap
summary: He answers questions on the strap, wooden pedal and packing of the overhead trap, names Slingerland as maker, and tells how it was stolen.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: How was that strap fastened to the beater itself? Did it go around the mall? No.
They had a, they had a, in the back of the ball, you see, they had a little hook, you see, and this foot pedal here would come up, you see, that strap would come up and hook that beater, you see.
In front of the beater or in back of the beater?
In the back of the beater. In the back of the beater. You see, when you go down, that would make it hit the bass drum, you see, and the spring would pull it back.
You understand what I mean? Yeah, I understand. And the foot pedal was made out of wood.
Yeah. It was wood, you see. And it screwed on the drum.
Did the foot pedal have a spring underneath it, or was it all worked from that one spring?

No, it worked from that one spring. You see, the spring here, with the hook here, and the beater, you hook the beater here, it would be straight up, and then you hook that other piece right back here, and bring that spring over, where I would cock the beater out. Uh-huh. And to get the beater here, when you take that strap, was on the, on the wooden pedal, you hook on there, and when you hit down, it would hit the bass drum.
The thing would go up like this, wouldn't you?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, I understand. You're trying to pull the pedal up? Yeah, the spring here would pull it back.
Now, when you put your drums away, did you have to disassemble all that?

No, you had to do on hook the spring, you see. I had to hook the spring, you see. In other words, relax it. Yeah. Instead of kicking up, this on hook, it would stay down, and you would just take that block, that wooden block, you didn't even put it in your case. You take that wooden block, and you'd wrap it up, and you'd put it right on the drum. You'd take your strap, and when you're holding the drum, keep it from sliding away from the chair, and you'd just wrap it around it.
Do you remember what make it was? Who made it?

It was the Slingerland. A Slingerland? Yeah, it was the Slingerland. Yeah, it was the Slingerland. It was the old make. It was the Slingerland. But that thing was beautiful. And I kept it just like new. Them guys just took it. I never could find out where it went. Never could find out. I was with Lee Collins one night, and he told me he seen a cat down at 31st Estate. That's where the Union Hall was at in Chicago, you know? Oh yeah. You see a fella with a trap wrapped up, but he didn't know if it was his or not. I said, I'd like to see him, because I had some files grooved in on that rod. I filed it, you know, in the back. I filed three little grooves in the back of it. Because if I'd have found him with it, I should have got him. Got him, got my beater from him. You better believe it. And them guys, they go around to pick up on those kind of things. You never see them no more.

It was really number one, very fun. You never have to change the rod or nothing. It's the middle of the ball you have to change. A lighter ball or a bigger ball. Always kept the two ball beaters, you know? You could take them off. You ain't put them off, you see?
